# Geometric mode control and an exponential coefficient comparison

All exponential variables in this note are independent and have mean one.
Gamma(k) denotes a sum of k such variables, with k a positive integer.
The results below concern exact scalar probabilities. They do not assert
that arbitrary simplex normals, convex fibers, or mixed-integer bodies
can be reduced to the coefficient patterns considered here.

## 1. Conditional means for sums of geometric variables

Let N_i be independent geometric random variables on the nonnegative
integers, with means b_i>0. Thus their probability masses are

    Pr(N_i=j)=(1-lambda_i)lambda_i^j,
    lambda_i=b_i/(1+b_i).

Put N=sum_i N_i, p(n)=Pr(N=n), and mu=sum_i b_i. Then p(n)>0
for every n>=0. For each i the conditional means

    m_i(n)=E[N_i | N=n]

are nondecreasing, and their increments satisfy

    0<=m_i(n)-m_i(n-1)<=1,
    sum_i[m_i(n)-m_i(n-1)]=1                       (n>=1).       (1)

Here is an elementary justification of the log-concavity input and the
conditional assertion. A nonnegative sequence without internal zeros
is log-concave precisely when its successive positive ratios decrease.
Its Toeplitz matrix T_(r,s)=a_(s-r), with a_j=0 for j<0, then has every
two-by-two minor nonnegative: the two middle-index factors dominate
the two extreme-index factors by the decreasing-ratio property. The
converse follows from consecutive minors. Convolution corresponds to
matrix multiplication. For any specified minor all nonzero intermediate
indices lie in a finite interval, and the two-by-two Cauchy--Binet
formula expresses the product minor as a sum of products of nonnegative
minors. Thus convolution preserves log-concavity and absence of gaps.
In particular every sum of the N_i has a log-concave probability mass.

If there is only one variable, (1) is immediate. Otherwise let r be the
mass function of the sum of all variables other than i. The conditional
law g_n(j) of N_i given N=n is proportional to
lambda_i^j r(n-j). Log-concavity of r, including its zero extension,
gives, for u<v,

    g_(n+1)(v)g_n(u)>=g_(n+1)(u)g_n(v).

Multiply this inequality by v-u and sum over u<v. Expanding the two
finite products shows that E_(g_(n+1))[j]>=E_(g_n)[j]. Hence every m_i
is nondecreasing. Their sum is n, so their nonnegative increments sum
to one. This proves (1), including all endpoint supports.

## 2. A discrete mode bound

Let b_max=max_i b_i. The preceding sum satisfies

    p(n)>=p(n-1) whenever 1<=n<=mu-b_max.                      (2)

For a geometric variable, shifting its defining series by one proves
the summation-by-parts identity

    E[(N_i-b_i)phi(N)]
      =b_i E[(N_i+1)(phi(N+1)-phi(N))].

It suffices here to use finitely supported phi, so convergence causes
no difficulty. Define

    tau(n)=sum_i b_i(m_i(n)+1)>0.

Sum the identity over i and take phi to be the indicator of n. This
gives the exact recurrence

    tau(n-1)p(n-1)=[tau(n)+n-mu]p(n).                        (3)

By (1), tau(n)-tau(n-1)<=b_max. For the n in (2), the bracket
in (3) is therefore at most tau(n-1). Both it and p(n) are positive,
as also follows from (3). Dividing proves (2). Coefficients b_i=0 may
be discarded, or regarded as deterministic zero variables.

## 3. A derivative sign for a gamma density convolved with negative phases

Let k>=2 and let

    Y=sum_i b_i E_i,       0<=b_i<=1,       sum_i b_i>=k.

If f is the density of Gamma(k)-Y, then

    f'(0)<=0.                                               (4)

The gamma density is g_k(x)=x^(k-1)e^(-x)/(k-1)! for x>0,
extended by zero for x<0. Since Y>0 almost surely and g_k has a
bounded derivative on the positive halfline,

    f'(0)=E[g_k'(Y)]
      =E[e^(-Y)((k-1)Y^(k-2)-Y^(k-1))]/(k-1)!.

At k=2 differentiation still follows by the global Lipschitz bound
on g_k and dominated convergence; Y=0 has probability zero.

Exponential tilting by e^(-Y) changes each b_i E_i to an exponential
of mean lambda_i=b_i/(1+b_i). Its Laplace normalizing factor is
L=product_i(1+b_i)^(-1)>0. Write h_r(lambda) for the complete
homogeneous polynomial of degree r, with h_0=1. Expanding moments
of independent exponentials gives

    E[e^(-Y)Y^r]=L r! h_r(lambda).

Consequently f'(0)=L[h_(k-2)(lambda)-h_(k-1)(lambda)]. The geometric
variables with means b_i have

    p(n)=product_i(1-lambda_i) h_n(lambda).

Their mean is at least k and their largest mean is at most one.
Apply (2) at n=k-1 to obtain h_(k-1)>=h_(k-2). This proves (4).

## 4. Equalization of negative coefficients with saturated positives

Fix k>=2 and an integer q>=k-1. For b=(b_1,...,b_q) satisfying

    0<=b_i<=1,       sum_i b_i=k-1,

define

    P_k(b)=Pr(Gamma(k)>=E_0+sum_i b_i E_i).

Then

    P_k(b)>=Pr(Gamma(k)>=E_0+((k-1)/q)Gamma(q)).               (5)

First take all b_i>0. Write V=Gamma(k)-E_0-sum_i b_iE_i.
Differentiation under the expectation, justified by the bounded gamma
density and the finite first exponential moments, and exponential
size bias give

    partial_(b_i) P_k=-f_(V-b_i E_i')(0),

where primes mean additional independent phases. Put
W=V-b_iE_i'-b_jE_j'. If W=X-bE' with X independent of E', direct
differentiation of the convolution integral gives
-b f_W'+f_W=f_X. Here X means the law with that particular extra
negative phase removed, not a new independent positive phase added.
Subtract the identities removing the two added phases:

    partial_(b_i)P_k-partial_(b_j)P_k
       =-(b_i-b_j)f_W'(0).                                  (6)

All density derivatives here exist; alternatively they follow directly
by averaging the bounded positive-halfline gamma derivative as in
Section 3. The total of the negative coefficients in W is
k+b_i+b_j, and each coefficient is at most one. Hence (4) makes
f_W'(0)<=0. Equation (6) shows that transferring mass from a smaller
coefficient to a larger one cannot decrease P_k, as long as the sum
and box constraints remain satisfied.

Conversely, transfer mass from a coefficient above (k-1)/q to one
below it, stopping when one reaches that average. Their order does
not reverse during the transfer, so P_k cannot increase. At least one
additional coordinate is fixed at the average each time. After
finitely many transfers every coordinate equals the average. This
proves (5). If some b_i vanish, first take their convex combination
with the positive equal vector and pass to the limit. Using the same
independent exponentials gives almost-sure convergence off the null
equality event, so bounded convergence proves (5) on the closed domain.

## 5. An exact lower bound independent of the number of negative phases

The right side of (5) decreases as q increases. Indeed, pad a vector
of q equal coefficients by one zero coefficient and apply (5) with
q+1 coordinates. Moreover the random variable ((k-1)/q)Gamma(q)
has mean k-1 and variance (k-1)^2/q, so it converges in probability
to k-1. The independent continuous law of Gamma(k)-E_0 then gives

    P_k(b)>=G_k:=Pr(Gamma(k)>=E_0+k-1).                        (7)

For completeness, convergence of the probabilities follows by trapping
the moving threshold between k-1-epsilon and k-1+epsilon outside an
event whose probability tends to zero, then letting epsilon decrease
to zero. The limiting threshold has no atom under Gamma(k)-E_0.

Integrating the integer-shape gamma survival function against E_0
gives the completely explicit expression

    G_k=e^(-(k-1)) sum_(j=0)^(k-1)
          ((k-1)^j/j!)(1-2^(-(k-j))).                         (8)

One can also obtain (8) by writing
Pr(Gamma(k)>=E_0+s)=Pr(Gamma(k)>=s)
-e^s E[e^(-Gamma(k))1_{Gamma(k)>=s}] and evaluating the two gamma
tails at s=k-1. In particular G_2=5/(4e) and G_3=27/(8e^2).

The case k=1 has no remaining negative mass and probability 1/2.
No universal numerical bound for all the G_k is claimed in this note.
More importantly, the premise that all positive coefficients equal one
has not been established for a general bounded-coefficient minimizer.
That premise is essential to the proof, through the integer gamma
density and the geometric recurrence above.
